claim: Meghalaya's living root bridges are grown from the living aerial roots of one tree species, Ficus elastica (the India rubber tree), trained across rivers by local people.

evidence.quote: which are grown with aerial roots of Ficus elastica
India rubber tree-based bridge construction near Cherrapunji

notes: Two independent owners agree on the species.

claim: They are grown by Khasi communities (the paper says the Khasi and Jaintia Hills); India's UNESCO submission credits 'indigenous Khasi tribal communities'.

evidence.quote: Grown by indigenous Khasi tribal communities
In the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, inhabitants of isolated villages have devised a practical and sustainable way of constructing living bridges

notes: Say 'Khasi villages' or 'villages in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills'; do not name other communities.

claim: The bridges get stronger as they grow: the roots thicken (secondary growth) and fuse with each other (inosculation).

evidence.quote: which strengthen themselves over time due to adaptive secondary growth and their capacity to form a mechanically stable structure via inosculations
Validating their increasing strength and ingenious use of root inosculation

claim: The 2015-2017 field survey measured bridges from 2 m to 52.7 m long; almost 80% (58 of 73 measured lengths) are shorter than 20 m.

evidence.quote: display a length of 2 to 52.7 m
58 of 73 measured lengths, or almost 80%, are shorter than 20 m

notes: Longest = Rangthylliang 12 (#37, Wah Pynursla), Table S1. Our parse of Table S1 finds 72 of the 73 lengths (one row lost in .docx conversion); the paper's own figures are used.

claim: Some bridges are several hundred years old; the Nongriat double-decker is put at about 200 years by the people who maintain it.

evidence.quote: Some bridges are several hundreds of years old
the bridge in Nongriat village (#6) is estimated to be ca. 200 years old

notes: Ages are estimates from residents' accounts, not dated. Hedge: 'about', 'by local account'. S02 says 'for centuries'.

claim: A bridge at Siej (#50) had been growing for 66 years and was still not fully usable when surveyed; scientists say the data do not yet allow a statement of how long a bridge takes to grow.

evidence.quote: The example of still not fully functional bridge number #50 with its growth time of already 66 years gives a first idea
So far, data do not allow for a statement on the time needed from beginning of construction

notes: Our measurement: ages refer to 2017/2018 (Table S1 footnote), so Siej was started about 1951-52.

claim: India submitted 'Jingkieng jri: Living Root Bridge Cultural Landscapes' to UNESCO's Tentative List on 17 Feb 2022; it is on the Tentative List, not the World Heritage List.

evidence.quote: Submitted by: Permanent Delegation of India to UNESCO

notes: Tentative List = candidate only. The same page lists 72 village entries (some grouping several villages) while the text says 'more than 75 remote villages'.

claim: According to India's UNESCO submission, Khasi belief says only an elder who has no children can plant the Ficus sapling for a root bridge.

evidence.quote: As per indigenous belief, only an elder, who has no children, can plant the Ficus sapling for a Living Root Bridge.

notes: Single source (State Party). Attribute it: 'India's UNESCO file says...'. Not in S01. Wording risk: present as a belief, not a universal rule.

claim: The survey geolocated 71 bridges; 68 of them lie in the rainforest valleys. Our measurement: they spread about 41 km west to east and 17 km south to north.

evidence.quote: 68 of the 71 geo-located bridges are located in the rainforest valleys

notes: Span figures are our measurement: method/rootbridge_numbers_output.txt (S1 west-east span km 41.2; south-north 17.3).
